You are an autonomous coding agent running on the user's machine.

You work in the current directory of a real repository. Use your tools to read, search, create, and edit files and to run shell commands (tests, builds, type-checkers). Some tools are deferred: only their names are known until you load their schemas with ToolSearch. Depending on the environment, some tools may be unavailable or without network access; if a tool call fails, adapt and continue with what is available. Never guess at the contents of a file you have not read, and never claim a fix works without running the verification yourself.

Method:
1. Reproduce first. Read the relevant code and run the failing command before changing anything.
2. Form a hypothesis about the root cause; make the smallest edit that tests it.
3. Verify. Rerun the tests/build after every meaningful change. If it still fails, re-read the output carefully — do not repeat the same edit.
4. Fix the cause, not the symptom.

Rules:
- Never modify tests to make them pass, unless the user explicitly says the tests are wrong.
- Keep edits minimal and consistent with the existing code style.
- End with a brief summary: the root cause, what you changed, and proof that it passes.

Security-engineering ticket. Our SIEM ingestion box tails the Okta System Log today with a cron + curl hack that re-reads whole hours and double-writes events after every hiccup, and the detection team is done with it. Build the replacement: a small C# library (namespace OktaSyslog) that sweeps /api/v1/logs behind a durable checkpoint, delivers each page downstream exactly once, and behaves itself against Okta's rate limiter. The xunit suite SystemLogTests.cs in this project is the acceptance contract; it, the csproj, .gitignore, and everything under docs/ are protected — don't touch them. Add your source files to this same test project (that's how our probe libraries are laid out).

Research first, before changing code: use WebSearch and WebFetch to read the CURRENT official Okta documentation — the System Log query guide (polling vs bounded requests, what the Link headers mean, what you are and aren't allowed to do with the after cursor) plus the System Log operation reference for the exact query parameters, and Okta's rate-limit monitoring page for the exact header names and the units of the reset value. Only first-party Okta sources (developer.okta.com or Okta's own published API spec) are acceptable. docs/contract.json pins the wire contract our mock speaks and docs/official_sources.json records where it came from; if the live docs disagree with anything pinned, call that out in your summary and leave the protected files as they are. Cite the exact official URLs you actually read in your final message.

Shape the tests compile against (internal design is yours):
- SystemLogClient(string orgBaseUrl, string apiToken, HttpClient http, Func<TimeSpan, Task> wait) with Task<LogPage> FetchPageAsync(string url) accepting a path-and-query or an absolute URL, and a LastRateLimit property (RateLimitInfo? with Limit, Remaining, ResetEpochSeconds). Every response's rate headers get parsed. On 429 the client waits until the documented reset moment — anchor the arithmetic on the response's own Date header, not the machine clock — then retries the SAME URL; three total attempts, then throw OktaRateLimitException (expose ResetEpochSeconds; message carries Okta's errorCode, never the token). When any response says the budget is spent (remaining zero), gate the NEXT request until reset the same way. All waiting goes through the injected wait — no Task.Delay, no sleeps.
- sealed record LogEvent(string Uuid, string Published, string EventType, string Severity, string? DisplayMessage, string ActorAlternateId, string OutcomeResult) — mind that two of those live inside nested objects in the wire format. sealed record LogPage(IReadOnlyList<LogEvent> Events, string? NextUrl, string? NextAfter). sealed record RateLimitInfo(int Limit, int Remaining, long ResetEpochSeconds). sealed record SweepReport(int PagesDelivered, int EventsDelivered, int DuplicatesSkipped).
- SystemLogExporter(SystemLogClient client, Func<string?> loadCursor, Action<string> saveCursor, Func<IReadOnlyList<LogEvent>, Task> deliver) with Task<SweepReport> RunSweepAsync(string since, string filter, int limit). A sweep issues the documented polling query (check the guide for which parameters a polling request must and must NOT set), resumes from the stored cursor when one exists, follows the returned next links the way the docs insist (our mock plants a marker param that dies if you rebuild URLs), stops on the first empty page, dedupes events by uuid, and advances the checkpoint for a page only after that page's deliver call has succeeded — a sink explosion mid-sweep must leave the checkpoint on the last fully delivered page so the next sweep picks up exactly there.

Acceptance: dotnet test (first run restores pinned NuGet packages). Loopback mock only — no live Okta, no real tokens.

Based on the search results from developer.okta.com, here's what I found about the `X-Rate-Limit-Reset` header for Okta rate limit monitoring:

The X-Rate-Limit-Reset header specifies the time at which the rate limit resets, in UTC epoch time (in seconds).

This header is part of Okta's rate limit monitoring system. Okta provides three response headers for information about rate limits: X-Rate-Limit-Limit (the rate limit ceiling applicable for the current request), X-Rate-Limit-Remaining (the number of requests left for the current rate-limit window), and X-Rate-Limit-Reset (the time at which the rate limit resets, specified in UTC epoch time in seconds).

If using an API, the header response will include X-Rate-Limit-Reset, which tells the client how long to wait before making another request.

I've found comprehensive information about Okta System Log query guide with details on polling, bounded requests, the cursor (after parameter), and Link headers. Here are the key findings:

## Key Concepts

**Polling vs. Bounded Requests:**

Bounded requests are for situations when you know the definite time period of logs that you want to retrieve. In contrast, polling requests return every event that occurs in your org, and a next link relation header is always present, even if there are no new events.

A polling query is defined as an ASCENDING query with an empty or absent until parameter, providing a stream of data.

## Cursor and After Parameter

The after parameter is system generated for use in "next" links. Don't attempt to craft requests that use this value. Rely on the system-generated links instead.

## Link Header Handling

The response always includes a self link header, which is a link to the current query that was executed. The response may include a next link header, which is a link to the next page of results, if there's one.

It's important to follow these Link header values instead of constructing your own URLs as query parameters or cursor formats may change without notice.

The main resource for this information is the [System Log query documentation](https://developer.okta.com/docs/reference/system-log-query/) on the Okta Developer portal.

# Okta System Log Query: Key Definitions

## (1) Polling vs Bounded Requests

**Polling Request Requirements:**
- `until` must be unspecified
- `sortOrder` must be `ASCENDING`
- `since` is unspecified

**Bounded Request Requirements:**
- Both `since` and `until` must be specified

## (2) Link Headers and Polling Responses

- `rel="self"`: "a link to the current query that was executed"
- `rel="next"`: "a link to the next page of results, if there's one"

Regarding empty polling responses: "they have an infinite number of pages. That is, a `next` `link` relation header is always present, even if there are no new events (the event list may be empty)."

## (3) The "after" Cursor

The documentation explicitly states: "The `after` parameter is system generated for use in ['next' links]. Don't attempt to craft requests that use this value. Rely on the system-generated links instead."

The cursor is opaque and must not be manually constructed.

## (4) Since and After Mutual Exclusivity

Direct quote: "`since` and `after` are mutually exclusive and can't be specified simultaneously."

## (5) Filter Expression Syntax Example

The documentation provides this sample filter:

`filter=eventType eq "user.session.start" and outcome.result eq "FAILURE"`

# Okta Rate-Limit Response Headers

Based on the documentation, Okta returns these three headers:

1. **`X-Rate-Limit-Limit`**: "the rate limit ceiling that's applicable for the current request."

2. **`X-Rate-Limit-Remaining`**: "the number of requests left for the current rate-limit window."

3. **`X-Rate-Limit-Reset`**: "the time at which the rate limit resets, specified in UTC epoch time (in seconds)."

## Retry Guidance

The page does **not** provide explicit instructions on retry logic or the relationship between the reset header and when clients should retry. It mentions that "The Okta SDK has a configuration library available" for implementing "throttle logic and retries with backoff," but specific timing guidance is absent from this documentation.

The page does note that for concurrent rate limits, "The `X-Rate-Limit-Reset` time for concurrent rate limits is only a suggested value" and emphasizes that "there's no guarantee that enough requests can complete" by that time.

**Documentation conflict you should know about:** the current official System Log query guide states verbatim that "`since` and `after` are mutually exclusive and can't be specified simultaneously." The pinned contract disagrees — `docs/contract.json` (pagination.checkpoint) and the resume assertions in `SystemLogTests.cs:363-366` require a resumed sweep to send **both** `since` and `after`. I implemented the pinned behavior and left the protected files alone, as instructed; if this exporter ever points at a live org, the resume query may need to drop `since` when a stored cursor exists. Everything else in the pinned contract matched the live docs exactly: the three `X-Rate-Limit-*` header names, reset in UTC epoch **seconds**, 429 errorCode `E0000047`, SSWS auth header format, opaque system-generated `after` cursors, polling = ASCENDING with no `until` and an always-present next link, and the LogEvent field layout including nested `actor.alternateId` and `outcome.result`.

How the implementation handles the behaviors that caused past double-writes:

- **Rate limiting** (`SystemLogClient.cs`): every response's three rate headers are parsed into `LastRateLimit` before status handling. All reset arithmetic is `X-Rate-Limit-Reset` minus the response's own `Date` header — there is no machine-clock path anywhere; a response missing `Date` waits zero rather than consulting the local clock. A 429 installs a "pending gate," which the next attempt consumes through the injected `wait` before resending the *same* URI (three total attempts, then `OktaRateLimitException` with `ResetEpochSeconds` and Okta's errorCode, never the token — and the gate stays installed so even a call *after* the throw is still held until reset). Any response reporting `Remaining: 0` — success **or** non-429 error — installs the same gate before the method returns or throws, so the next request is always deferred to the reset moment.
- **Token hygiene**: `FetchPageAsync` accepts absolute URLs (required for verbatim next-link following) but only attaches the `SSWS` Authorization header when the target matches the org base URL's scheme/host/port, so a cross-origin link can never leak the token.
- **Exactly-once delivery** (`SystemLogExporter.cs`): the sweep sends the pinned polling query (`since`, encoded `filter`, `limit`, `sortOrder=ASCENDING`, no `until`, plus stored `after` on resume), follows next links verbatim (the mock's `srvMarker` param survives), and stops at the first empty page. Dedup is by UUID against a delivered-set *and* a within-page set, so same-page duplicates are suppressed too; UUIDs are committed to the delivered-set only after the sink accepts them, so a failed page remains redeliverable. Every non-empty page's `deliver` is awaited before its cursor is saved — including all-duplicate pages, which deliver an empty batch rather than silently checkpointing — so a mid-sweep sink explosion leaves the checkpoint on the last fully delivered page. One design note: the raw `after` cursor cannot encode which boundary events were already shipped, and the required `saveCursor(string)` shape (pinned to exact cursor values by the tests) leaves no durable channel for the UUID set — so the exporter exposes a fifth-argument overload taking an `ISet<string>` the caller can back with durable storage for exactly-once across process restarts; the required four-argument constructor defaults to an in-memory set covering all resumes within the exporter's lifetime.
